Looking at both chapter pairs carefully, I'll apply each test systematically.

**Ch 005 Draft Analysis:**

The draft opens mentioning "their uncle's sermons" — the uncle (Dr. Frothingham) was an authorized removal, but the phrase "their uncle" still parses because "innumerable cousins" establishes a family context and readers can infer a familial preacher. Borderline, but a competent reader would not be confused — they'd understand some clerical uncle is meant.

"The critics called him cold" — the source has "The same thing might perhaps have been said of John Quincy Adams, but in him his associates averred that it was accompanied by mental restlessness… No one ever charged Charles Francis Adams with this fault. The critics charged him with just the opposite defect. They called him cold." The draft cuts the setup entirely, leaving "The critics called him cold" as a broken pivot — the preceding draft paragraph praises his balance with no contrasting charge, so "called him cold" arrives with no logical antecedent contrast. However, examining more carefully: the draft says "The world never loved perfect poise" and describes what "perfect poise" costs — the "cold" remark follows as a consequence of that argument. A competent reader can still track the logic. Not a genuine confusion.

"Of the four men, Dana was the most marked" — the draft counts Palfrey, Dana, Sumner, plus Adams himself as the fourth. Source says "of the four men" referring to Adams, Palfrey, Dana, Sumner. Draft has described only three (Palfrey, Dana, Sumner) before this sentence, since Adams's role as the group's center was established earlier. A reader can infer Adams is the fourth. Not a genuine confusion.

**Ch 006 Draft Analysis:**

"Only in one way did he render great service: trying to teach him French." — The pronoun "he" here refers to the father. The preceding sentence is "His father made no effort to force his mind, but left him free play." So "he" = the father is clear. No issue.

The draft omits the source's passage about Latin/Greek vs. the four tools, and the "had his father kept the boy at home" counterfactual. The remaining sentence "These four tools were necessary to his success in life, but he never controlled any one of them" still parses fine.

After careful review of both drafts against all six tests and the gate test, I find no structurally damaged sentences that would genuinely confuse a competent reader without source access. The compressions produce a less ornamented text, but no broken referential chains, dangling pronouns without antecedents in the draft, broken logical pivots where one side is missing, missing definitional glosses that block comprehension, unattributed dialogue, or mid-scene jumps meeting the defined criteria.
